questions.question: A small draft model proposes K tokens and a large target verifies them in one forward pass. What is the central benefit?
options: The target skips verification whenever the draft is smaller.
A correct prefix yields several target-distributed tokens per target pass.
The accepted tokens become independent of the target distribution.
The draft replaces the target, so no quality comparison is needed.
questions.explanation: A cheap draft proposes a prefix, and the target verifies several positions in one forward pass. The rejection rule corrects mismatches so emitted samples still follow the target distribution; the draft speeds sampling but does not replace the target’s quality check.

questions.question: For a proposed token, the target probability is p=0.3 and the draft probability is q=0.6. Under the lesson's acceptance rule, what probability accepts it?
options: 1.0, because p is smaller than q.
0.3, because acceptance equals target probability.
2.0, from q/p before clipping.
0.5, from min(1,p/q).
questions.explanation: The acceptance probability is min(1,p/q)=min(1,0.3/0.6)=0.5. Reversing the ratio gives q/p=2, which clips to 1 and would accept every proposal, so the numerator must be the target probability. The ratio measures target support for the draft token.

questions.question: At a rejected position, target distribution p=[0.6,0.4] and draft distribution q=[0.8,0.2]. What replacement distribution comes from the positive residual?
options: [1, 0], because q-p is [0.2,0] before normalization.
[0.6, 0.4], because the residual is always the target distribution.
[0.8, 0.2], because the residual is always the draft distribution.
[0, 1], because max(p-q,0) is [0,0.2] before normalization.
questions.explanation: On rejection, take the positive part of p−q: [max(0,0.6−0.8), max(0,0.4−0.2)]=[0,0.2]. Its sum is 0.2, so normalization gives [0,1], restoring target mass the draft underrepresented; only where p exceeds q is residual mass available.

questions.question: With acceptance rate alpha=0.8 and draft length K=4, what is the expected number of tokens emitted per target verification pass?
options: About 4.00 tokens, because four drafts are proposed.
About 5.00 tokens, because K+1 is always emitted.
About 2.56 tokens, from alpha times K.
questions.explanation: Expected output is (1−α^(K+1))/(1−α), the sum 1+α+…+α^K for accepted-prefix lengths. With α=0.8 and K=4, (1−0.8^5)/0.2=3.3616 tokens per pass; the terms count probabilities of accepting zero through four drafts, five possible prefix lengths.

questions.question: An EAGLE draft produces a candidate tree instead of a single chain. What attention mask should the target use to verify it?
options: A fully bidirectional mask where every candidate sees every other candidate.
A padding mask that removes every candidate after the root.
A tree-causal mask where each candidate attends only to its ancestors.
A sliding-window mask that lets each candidate see only the last token.
questions.explanation: A tree-causal mask lets each candidate attend along its own ancestor path, preserving causal context while preventing sibling branches from leaking into one another. A fully bidirectional mask would mix competing candidates during verification.

questions.question: A service runs high-temperature creative sampling, where draft-target agreement is low. What deployment effect should it monitor?
options: Draft overhead may outweigh the low accepted-token count and reduce speed.
The target will always accept more tokens as temperature rises.
The tree mask will convert low acceptance into guaranteed speedup.
The rejection rule becomes approximate and changes the target distribution.
questions.explanation: High temperature makes draft and target distributions less aligned, reducing acceptance; measure accepted tokens per verify and actual wall time because draft cost may exceed the savings. Rejection sampling remains exact even when it is not faster.
